brief.situation: 10:30 in an outpatient clinic. You are the physical therapist assistant, carrying out the physical therapist's plan. Mr. Ibrahim, 71, is on visit 6 of a conditioning program after a heart attack. Today's plan steps the treadmill grade up every 2 minutes.
handover: Plan of care (Dr. Moreno, PT): treadmill intervals with the grade increased every 2 minutes, perceived exertion 11-13, blood pressure and heart rate each stage. Takes a beta-blocker.
The plan's stopping rules: a systolic drop of more than 10 mmHg as the workload rises, chest discomfort, new dysrhythmia, dizziness or SpO2 under 90%; stop, seat the patient, and tell the PT at once.
Dr. Moreno is in the clinic; the clinic has an automated defibrillator.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Each question or measure takes the time on its button. Decide what to collect, what it means for today's session and who needs to know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Mr. Ibrahim's systolic is falling as the grade goes up, and he is lightheaded. What does it mean, and who decides?

parts.label: What the data show
parts.criteria: Systolic pressure should rise with workload (about 10 per MET); a fall of more than 10 as work rises, with lightheadedness, two months after a heart attack, is an abnormal response and a stopping rule; the beta-blocker blunts heart rate, so pressure matters more.
parts.modelAnswer: His systolic should rise with the work, but it has dropped by more than 10 and he's lightheaded. After a heart attack that's an abnormal response and one of the plan's stopping rules.

parts.label: What I do and who decides
parts.criteria: Stops and seats him; defibrillator at hand; tells the PT now with the data; the PT reexamines and decides; documents data.
parts.modelAnswer: I stop the treadmill, sit him down, bring the defibrillator, and get Dr. Moreno now. The reexamination and plan change are hers; I document the numbers and times.

scoring.modelReasoning: During graded exercise systolic pressure should rise, about 10 mmHg per MET. Two months after a heart attack, on a beta-blocker that blunts heart rate, a systolic that falls more than 10 as the grade rises, with lightheadedness, is a stopping rule. The PTA stops and seats him, brings the defibrillator and tells the supervising PT at once with the numbers; the PT reexamines and decides.

sbpQ.ask: While you check the stage: how should systolic pressure respond as workload rises?

choices.label: It rises, about 10 mmHg per MET

sbpQ.explain: Normal exercise response: SBP rises about 10 mmHg per MET; a drop over 10 mmHg with increasing workload is a stop criterion.
